features.feature_value: Used anger/cursing/name-calling to decide rejection; allowed if opinion/questions without strict name-calling and tied to the topic.
features.evidence_span: I first looked at the language of the post... reject the post... angry with curse words or blatant name calling... However if the post stated an opinion, or posed questions without strictly name calling... i allowed both.
features.rationale: The participant explicitly describes a language-based rule for rejecting vs allowing.

features.feature_value: Rejected posts that felt like personal/side attacks rather than spreading information; allowed opinion but not mud-dragging.
features.evidence_span: If it felt it was more of an attack as opposed to an attempt to spread "information", I said not to allow... do we have to drag names through the mud, do we have to attack the other side.
features.rationale: They set an explicit attack-vs-information criterion grounded in the reflection text.

features.feature_value: Allowed almost everything under free-speech absolutism; removed mainly when posts were attacking or seemed not thoughtful.
features.evidence_span: I am quite the free speech absolutist. I allowed almost every post, except when they were attacking, or seemed just reacting from a bad place, not a thoughtful one.
features.rationale: Their stated policy is strongly tied to allowing vs removing based on attack/nonthoughtful framing.

features.feature_value: Disliked censorship concepts; removed only for bad grammar/confusing syntax or insulting behavior.
features.evidence_span: I am anti-censorship. The term "hate speech" sounds like something out of Orwell's book 1984... remove both if the grammar was bad or the syntax was confusing or insulting took place.
features.rationale: They articulate a specific non-content, form/insult-only removal standard.

features.feature_value: Generally permitted free-speech even if not nice, but drew a line when posts were vulgar purely for vulgarity/over-the-top to prove a point.
features.evidence_span: most of them were okay (not nice) but free speech... there has to be a line somewhere when the post are just vulgar to be vulgar and over the top trying to prove their point.
features.rationale: They explicitly state a boundary condition for vulgarity.

features.feature_value: Usually kept both or removed both; wanted to remove only one when it was more offensive but always removed anything containing profanity.
features.evidence_span: I always removed anything with profanity.
features.rationale: The participant directly ties profanity to removal decisions.

features.feature_value: Used perspective-taking (Democrat vs Republican) to judge plausibility; removed claims they considered false that could harm readers.
features.evidence_span: I tried to see if these statements made sense putting myself in the head of a Democrat and republican, but eliminated those that I thought were false and could harm the readers.
features.rationale: They describe a specific comparative reasoning step and a harm/falsehood criterion.

features.feature_value: Split content by quality: some points as genuine viewpoint and others as nonsense for both sides.
features.evidence_span: Some points voiced a true viewpoint, while others expressed nonsense for both sides
features.rationale: The reflection explicitly differentiates “true viewpoint” from “nonsense,” implying content-quality discrimination.
